entries.question: Are miracles proof of divine mission?
entries.summary: Matthew 11:2-5 has Jesus point to his miracles — blind seeing, lame walking, lepers cleansed, deaf hearing, dead raised — as the answer to John the Baptist's question whether he is the coming one. John 3:2 has Nicodemus reason backward from Jesus' signs to the conclusion that no one could do them unless God were with him. Exodus 14:31 grounds Israelite faith in Moses in the great work at the Red Sea. The opposing side cites Exodus 7:10-12, where Pharaoh's magicians replicate Aaron's serpent-rod sign with their enchantments, Deuteronomy 13:1-3, which explicitly commands Israel to reject a prophet whose sign or wonder comes to pass if he calls them to other gods, and Luke 11:19, where Jesus concedes that Jewish exorcists also cast out demons. Miracles are evidentiary in the first set; the second set says miracles do not settle the question of divine authorization.
entries.commentary: This contradiction operates at the level of evidentiary epistemology and it is one of the more interesting ones in the canon because both sides are right about something. The pro-miracle stream — Matthew 11, John 3, Exodus 14 — treats sign-events as warrants for prophetic or messianic identity. The Matthean Jesus deflects John's question by reciting a list of healings that echoes Isaiah 35:5-6 and 61:1, framing the miracles as the fulfillment of messianic prophecy. The Johannine semeia theology is even more explicit — the signs are the basis on which the reader is asked to believe (John 20:30-31). Exodus 14:31 turns the Red Sea event into the foundation of Israel's covenant faith in Yahweh and Moses. But the counter-stream is just as clear. Exodus 7:10-12 puts the Egyptian magicians on the same evidentiary footing as Aaron — they too can produce serpents — which means the sign-event alone does not establish whose god is real. Deuteronomy 13:1-3 makes this explicit at the level of legal principle: even a fulfilled sign or wonder does not authenticate a prophet if his message contradicts covenant fidelity. Luke 11:19 has Jesus himself concede that Jewish exorcists who are not his disciples also perform exorcisms, which means exorcistic power is not by itself proof of his unique authorization. Apologists like Norman Geisler and Craig Blomberg harmonize by distinguishing between genuine and counterfeit miracles, arguing that Pharaoh's magicians performed lesser or demonic signs while Aaron's was true divine power, and that Deuteronomy 13 only applies when the prophet's message is heretical. The distinction is theologically convenient but exegetically strained — the Exodus narrative does not say the magicians' serpents were illusions or demonic; it says they did so as Aaron did, in like manner. The more parsimonious reading is that the Hebrew Bible and the New Testament both contain a more sophisticated epistemology than the pro-miracle proof-texts suggest. Miracles function as evidence in some contexts and are explicitly disqualified as standalone evidence in others. The contradiction is real at the level of any flat claim that miracles prove divine mission — Deuteronomy 13:1-3 is the smoking gun against that thesis, and it is in the same Torah that grounds Mosaic authority in the Red Sea sign.

answers.answer: Miracles are proof of divine missions
answers.answer_explanation:
Now when John had heard in the prison the works of Christ, he sent two of his disciples,

And said unto him, Art thou he that should come, or do we look for another?

Jesus answered and said unto them, Go and shew John again those things which ye do hear and see:

The blind receive their sight, and the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have the gospel preached to them.

The same came to Jesus by night, and said unto him, Rabbi, we know that thou art a teacher come from God: for no man can do these miracles that thou doest, except God be with him.

And Israel saw that great work which the LORD did upon the Egyptians: and the people feared the LORD, and believed the LORD, and his servant Moses.

answers.answer: Miracles are not proof of divine mission
answers.answer_explanation:
And Moses and Aaron went in unto Pharaoh, and they did so as the LORD had commanded: and Aaron cast down his rod before Pharaoh, and before his servants, and it became a serpent.

Then Pharaoh also called the wise men and the sorcerers: now the magicians of Egypt, they also did in like manner with their enchantments.

For they cast down every man his rod, and they became serpents: but Aaron's rod swallowed up their rods.

If there arise among you a prophet, or a dreamer of dreams, and giveth thee a sign or a wonder,

And the sign or the wonder come to pass, whereof he spake unto thee, saying, Let us go after other gods, which thou hast not known, and let us serve them;

Thou shalt not hearken unto the words of that prophet, or that dreamer of dreams: for the LORD your God proveth you, to know whether ye love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul.

And if I by Beelzebub cast out devils, by whom do your sons cast [them] out? therefore shall they be your judges.

commentary_out.commentary:
This is one of the more substantive theological tensions in the canon because both streams are partly correct, and the disagreement is epistemological rather than merely narrative: it concerns what a miracle is evidence *for*. The pro-evidentiary stream treats sign-events as warrants for prophetic or messianic identity. In Matthew 11:2-5 the imprisoned Baptist asks whether Jesus is 'the coming one' (ho erchomenos), and Jesus answers not with a claim but with a catalogue of deeds — blind seeing, lame walking, lepers cleansed, deaf hearing, dead raised, poor evangelized — that deliberately stitches together Isaiah 35:5-6 and 61:1. The miracles function as fulfilled prophecy; they are evidentiary precisely because they match a script. The Johannine theology is even more explicit. John's preferred term for Jesus' miracles is not dynameis ('mighty works') but sēmeia ('signs'), and Nicodemus in John 3:2 reasons exactly as the Evangelist wants the reader to: 'no one can do these signs unless God is with him.' The redactional purpose statement in John 20:30-31 makes the sēmeia the explicit ground of belief. Exodus 14:31 supplies the foundational Israelite instance: after the sea event the people 'feared the LORD and believed in the LORD and in Moses his servant.'

The counter-stream is equally canonical and arguably more theologically careful. Exodus 7:10-12 places the Egyptian ḥarṭummim ('magicians') on the same evidentiary footing as Aaron — they too throw down rods that become serpents — so the bare sign-event cannot adjudicate whose deity is real; only the swallowing of their rods does, and that is a contest of power, not a demonstration that signs authenticate. Deuteronomy 13:1-3 (13:2-4 in the Hebrew) raises this to legal principle: a prophet may give a sign or wonder (ʾôt or môpēt), the wonder may actually come to pass, and Israel is still commanded to reject him if he counsels apostasy — for 'the LORD your God is testing you.' This is the decisive text. It explicitly stipulates that a genuine, fulfilled wonder does not authenticate the messenger; content trumps spectacle. Luke 11:19, embedded in the Beelzebul controversy (Q material paralleled in Matthew 12:27), has Jesus concede that 'your sons' — Jewish exorcists outside his movement — also cast out demons, so exorcistic power is not by itself proof of his unique commission.

The standard harmonization, advanced by Norman Geisler and echoed by traditional commentators, distinguishes genuine from counterfeit miracles: Pharaoh's magicians worked lesser, demonic, or illusory feats, and Deuteronomy 13 engages only when the message is heretical. The Deuteronomy half of this is exegetically sound and is, in fact, the key to the whole problem — the text itself makes message-content the discriminator, which is a sophisticated epistemology, not a contradiction. The Egyptian-magician half is weaker: the narrative says the ḥarṭummim acted 'in like manner with their enchantments' (belahaṭêhem) and offers no textual cue that their serpents were tricks rather than real transformations; the differentiator the text supplies is Aaron's rod devouring theirs, i.e., superior power, not superior authenticity. Tigay and Propp both note the polemical thrust: the contest concedes the rivals' efficacy in order to assert Yahweh's supremacy. So the harmonization succeeds where it follows Deuteronomy's own logic and fails where it imports a later metaphysics of demonic counterfeits absent from the Exodus text.

Read together, the canon does not actually hold a flat 'miracles prove divine mission' doctrine. It holds that signs are necessary but not sufficient — corroborating evidence to be weighed against the prophet's message and fruit (Matthew 7:15-20; Deuteronomy 13). The tension is genuine only against the crude proof-text version; against the layered version both streams cohere. Verdict: partially harmonizable — the proof-texts overstate, but Deuteronomy 13 supplies the canon's own qualifying principle, and the residual friction is real chiefly in the Exodus magicians' parity.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The tension is real against any flat 'miracles prove divine mission' thesis, but it softens once both streams are read as a single, layered epistemology in which sign-events are necessary-but-not-sufficient evidence, weighed against the content of the message. Deuteronomy 13 does not deny that the false prophet's wonder occurs; it subordinates the sign to covenant fidelity, which is the same move the Synoptic Beelzebul saying makes when it appeals to the source and fruit of the power rather than the bare fact of it.

commentary_out.change_summary: Roughly doubled the commentary by adding original-language detail (semeia, harṭummim, môpēt), the Deut 13 vs Exod 14 Torah-internal tension, the Egyptian magician question, the Beelzebul pericope's redactional setting, the rabbinic and patristic discrimination criteria, and a sharper evaluation of the Geisler/Blomberg counterfeit-miracle move.
